newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: FEATURE-Colombia's businessmen split over peace with guerrillas.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Colombia's businessmen split over peace with guerrillas.

text.p: As Colombia's main leftist rebel army gains political and military momentum, conservative business leaders are split over whether to give peace a chance or let the country's internecine war rumble on.

President Ernesto Samper has won the unprecedented public backing of four of Colombia's leading industrialists for his recent proposal to seek a negotiated end to Latin America's longest-running guerrilla conflict.

But others say Samper, who hands over power next year after being severely weakened by a scandal stemming from his alleged ties to drug lords, is in no position to win concessions from hardline rebel leaders that could end a conflict costing billions of dollars per year.

"We believe we are truly interpreting the wish of...the business sector in particular by requesting that you take steps to start and implement the peace process," the four industrialists and financiers wrote in an open letter to Samper on June 19.
Following that call, the president announced a new push for peace in a televised speech on June 23 and dispatched two "peace envoys" to make contact with leftist rebel leaders within 60 days.
But just two days later two heads of the powerful Sindicato Antioqueno industrial conglomerate attacked Samper's initiative.

"I would say (the government) has extremely low credibility...Colombians do not believe the government is leading the country down the right path, including the path of peace," said Nicanor Restrepo, chairman of Sindicato flagship Suramericana de Seguros.

In a letter to the local press, Fabio Rico Calle, head of the Sindicato's Compania Nacional de Chocolates, wrote: "We all want peace, but to achieve it one must have unshakable resolve, sincerity and moral authority."
WAR COSTS FOUR PERCENT OF GDP A YEAR

The prospect of new peace negotiations arose as the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC), the country's oldest and largest rebel group, freed 70 troops in a temporarily demilitarized zone in southern Caqueta province on June 15.

The government presented the handover of the soldiers, some of whom were taken prisoner almost 10 months earlier, as a victory for dialogue. But political analysts widely saw it as the latest in a series of humiliating blows to the military.

According to a 1995 study by the government's National Planning Department, the guerrilla war cost Colombia about $12 billion between 1990 and 1994 -- equivalent to about 4 percent of gross domestic product per year.

"The economic groups want peace because they have probably concluded that it is cheaper than war...the main obstacle to economic development is the lack of peace," wrote commentator Patricia Lara in Cambio 16 political magazine.
But any lasting peace deal with the rebels seems likely to have a high political and economic cost.
The FARC's top leader Manuel "Sureshot" Marulanda in 1993 set out a 10-point plan for the creation of a government of "national reconstruction and reconciliation".
REBELS WANT MIXED ECONOMY, SWEEPING LAND REFORM
The plan lays out the FARC blueprint for "development and modernisation with social justice," demanding that 50 percent of the national budget be spent on social development programmes.

And while the FARC, set up as a pro-Soviet force in 1964, has said it would favour a mixed economy, it has insisted on a sweeping redistribution of wealth through agrarian reform and a key role for the state in strategic sectors of the economy, including the oil industry.

In a communique issued in mid-June, jailed leaders of the National Liberation Army (ELN), Colombia's second largest guerrilla force, described industrialists' backing for Samper's peace initiative as "of the greatest importance".
But the FARC does not appear to take the proposal at face value.
"For the ruling class, peace means the ability to continue ...exploiting the people," Joaquin Gomez, head of the FARC's so-called Southern Bloc, told Reuters in a recent interview.
Influential columnist Enrique Santos of the leading El Tiempo newspaper also voiced doubts over the growing calls for peace.
"It's naive to believe that a weak government, with a crisis of legitimacy at home and abroad and distanced from the military high command, is in any position to lead negotiations," he wrote.
GROWING REBEL, ARMY EQUILIBRIUM

Armed Forces chief General Harold Bedoya, who recently described the government as "extremely weak," has voiced disapproval of Samper's peace initiative and called for the "narco-subversives" to be defeated.
But if the military option wins over the political solution, there is little to indicate it will be any more successful now than over the last 30 years.

The defence budget has burgeoned, but so too have the guerrillas' ranks and firepower, leading to a growing balance between the state's unwieldy war machine and hit-and-run guerrilla armies with intimate knowledge of Colombia's mountains and vast jungles.
Independent analysts believe the rebel forces number some 18,000 and have de facto political and economic control of 50 percent of the country.
The army has an active fighting force of about 100,000, one-third of which is tied up protecting key oil infrastructure -- the frequent target of guerrilla attacks.
In the period from 1990 to 1994, the Planning Department calculated the country's three guerrilla forces reaped about $1.7 billion from drug trafficking, kidnapping and extortion.

In a recent Reuters interview, Samper said the FARC alone had earned more than $700 million from kidnapping and extortion in 1996 -- compared to the government's entire defence budget of $900 million for 1997.
One of the soldiers released after more than nine months in rebel hands commented on the guerrillas' growing strength: "The only things the FARC doesn't have are airplanes and tanks."
